vignette:
Rohan, a 26-year-old editor, found himself at a crossroads, his once vibrant life with his wife now shadowed by an pervasive sense of dread that had steadily tightened its grip since an incident with the police several months prior. He had been walking home late one evening, lost in thought after a long day at the publishing house, when he was suddenly cornered and roughly apprehended by officers who mistook him for a suspect in a nearby altercation. Pushed hard against a cold, grimy brick wall, his arms twisted behind his back, Rohan remembered the biting chill seeping into his skin. A female officer, her voice sharp and dismissive, had interrogated him, her presence dominating the terrifying encounter. He recalled feeling an eerie detachment, as if watching the scene unfold from a distance, completely powerless. He was held for hours in a small, frigid room, the stale air thick with the faint metallic scent of disinfectant, before being released without charge, the experience leaving an indelible mark.

In the months that followed, Rohan's world began to shrink. The specific temperature on his skin, even a slight chill in his air-conditioned office, could send a jolt of alarm through him, instantly reminding him of the cold wall and the cell. These tactile triggers, often innocuous, would often plunge him into a profound self-doubt, where he would ruminate on how his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, unable to handle even minor discomfort without spiraling. Similarly, being alone with women, particularly in quiet or confined spaces like a meeting room with a female colleague, became a potent trigger, bringing back the intimidating presence of the officer. This, too, fed his growing conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that danger lurked in every corner.

His escalating negative appraisals profoundly affected his inner world. Because he had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, his mind would invariably drift to the traumatic memory, not as a fleeting thought but as an immersive experience. When these memories came to mind, he would feel his body was in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, a visceral reenactment that left him gasping for breath and drenched in sweat. This physical reliving of the trauma, combined with an overwhelming grief on recall, only served to strengthen his appraisal that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. The sheer weight of the memory, bringing with it the grief and the unsettling feeling of his body being constrained, often confirmed his deepest fears about the futility of his existence.

This cycle was self-reinforcing. His deep-seated belief that nothing good could happen to him anymore made him hypervigilant, constantly scanning his environment, unconsciously seeking confirmation of his fears. This meant he was exquisitely sensitive to potential triggers, like the faintest drop in temperature in his office or the presence of a lone female colleague, which would then confirm his negative appraisals. When he thought about the frightening event, he would sometimes experience olfactory recall, catching a phantom whiff of the metallic disinfectant he smelt in the holding room. The sudden, vivid sensory experience of this memory made him acutely aware of any similar smells in his environment, turning them into potent triggers that would instantly transport him back to the trauma.

Rohan's work as an editor, which once brought him immense satisfaction, now felt like a constant battle. He found himself avoiding collaborative projects, especially those requiring one-on-one meetings with female authors or colleagues, damaging his professional reputation. His detachment, initially a coping mechanism during the trauma, now resurfaced as a dissociative feeling whenever he was stressed or triggered, making him feel unreal and further isolating him from his wife and his once-cherished routines. The constant internal struggle, the belief that he was a lousy coper and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, had eroded his enthusiasm, making him a shadow of his former self. It was this creeping despair, the feeling of a life slowly draining of color and purpose, that finally compelled Rohan to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the future he once envisioned.
